You use the passive and impersonal constructions at B2 level: ser + participle, estar + participle (result), passive se and impersonal se, the impersonal third person plural, and choose the structure that suits the register.
The launch has been moved to the morning.
All the copies have been sold.
They say there’s a huge queue.
At the fair people are talking about the two of them.
To form the passive with “ser + participle” (agreeing) and use it in written and formal registers.
To distinguish “ser + participle” (the action) from “estar + participle” (the result).
To use passive “se” (se venden libros) and impersonal “se” (se vive bien, se busca a alguien).
To use the impersonal third person plural (dicen que, llaman a la puerta).
To choose the right construction: the passive with “ser” is rare in speech; in conversation “se” or the active voice is preferred.

30 May, nine in the morning, the Retiro park. Because of the heat, the launch has been moved to the morning. Andrés has come in his wheelchair, accompanied by Marta. Ecaterina arrived half an hour early. The marquee is already full.
Everything is ready. The launch has been moved to ten, because of the heat.
And Costel’s books? Where are they?
They’ve been set out at the publisher’s stand. But they say there’s already a queue of more than a hundred people.
A hundred people? For a Romanian book? Nothing like that was ever seen in my bookshop.
It’s not the book, Andrés. It’s the story. The whole fair is talking about the two of us.
About us? And what are people saying?
They’re saying the bookseller waited forty years. And that the translator came to fetch her book.
(smiling) That’s true. Although I’d have told it better.
Look, Andrés: in the front row there are Costel, Andrei, Ana and Mihai. And the little girl has been sat on Costel’s knees.
(laughing) Ecaterina, you don’t say it like that. You say: “The little girl is sitting on Costel’s knees.”
You’re right. Nerves make me talk like a newspaper. Come on, let’s start before the books sell out.
“lo habría contado” = I would have told it
Listen to the ending: «trasladadO» / «trasladadA» / «trasladadOS» / «trasladadAS». In fast speech in Spain “-ado” sounds almost like “-ao”, but in writing and in the exam pronounce the “d” clearly.
“Se” is unstressed and links to the verb: [se-DI-ce], [se-VEN-den].
o-ba-SIÓN in Latin America, o-ba-THIÓN in Spain; stress on the last syllable.
“Ser” (in any tense) + participle AGREEING with the subject. The agent, if mentioned, is introduced with “por”:
The books were brought by a Romanian lorry driver.
The novel will be translated into English.

The passive with “ser” is much rarer in Spanish than in English. It appears mainly in the press and in official and scientific texts. In conversation it sounds stiff: Ecaterina talks “like a newspaper”.
La carpa fue montada ayer. (Someone put it up yesterday.)
La carpa está montada. (It’s ready; that’s how it is now.)
La puerta es abierta a las nueve. (process)
Los libros fueron colocados por Marta.
Los libros están colocados en la caseta.
Trick: if you can add “por + someone”, it’s an action (ser). If you’re describing how something is now, it’s a result (estar).
the verb agrees with the object
Se vende un libro. / Se venden libros.
verb in the singular, no subject
Se vive bien aquí. / Se habla de ellos.
a + person, verb in the singular
A common mistake: «Se vende pisos» ✗ → «Se venden pisos» ✓ (pisos is plural). But with people: «Se busca a dos camareros» (singular, because “a dos camareros” is not the subject).

Register: “Dicen que…” is the most natural in speech; “Se dice que…” is neutral; “Es sabido que…” or the passive with “ser” are for writing.
En la caseta de la editorial
¿Cuántas personas hay en la cola, según dicen?

A press report on the second day of the fair. Notice how the journalist uses the passive and constructions with “se”.

The second day of the Madrid Book Fair was marked by an unusual launch. At ten in the morning, the event, which had been moved because of the heat, brought together more than three hundred people in the main marquee.

The Romanian translation of a Madrid novel was being presented, a novel whose story has been followed by millions of people on social media. The hundred copies available, which had been transported from Bucharest by lorry, sold out in twenty minutes.
The presence of the real protagonist of the story, a former bookseller aged eighty-nine, was expected. When he was seen coming in in his wheelchair, the audience rose to its feet.
According to the organisers, such a long ovation had never been seen at the launch of a translation. It is said that even the sellers at the neighbouring stands stopped serving to listen.
¿En cuánto tiempo se agotaron los ejemplares?
¿Qué hicieron los vendedores de las casetas vecinas?

The plane from Bucharest landed at Barajas on 29 May at ten past eleven, twenty minutes late. Ecaterina had spent the whole flight with Rayuela open on her knees, without reading. Ana had noticed she didn’t turn a single page. Rosa Elena had slept for two hours straight, hugging the drawing of the book lorry, which she had refused to put in the suitcase because, according to her, important drawings are carried by hand.

At the arrivals gate a group was waiting for them that would have attracted attention at any airport in the world: a Romanian lorry driver in a freshly ironed shirt, a young photographer with three cameras round his neck, a writer with round glasses and, in the middle, Carmen and Juan, Ana’s parents, who had come from Lavapiés with a bunch of carnations. Juan was also carrying a bag of churros. He said they were “just in case”.

In the taxi to Lavapiés, Carmen sat next to Costel and subjected him to a full interrogation, with the seriousness of a judge. She asked him where he was from, how old he was, whether he was married and, above all, whether it was true he had taken soup to the translator for two weeks. Costel confessed that he hadn’t made the soup himself; his neighbour had. Carmen looked at him in silence for a few seconds and then told him that didn’t matter, because what counts with soup isn’t who cooks it but who brings it.

That afternoon, Ecaterina visited Andrés in the flat on the calle del Prado. Nobody else went into the living room. They were alone for two hours. When Ecaterina came out, her eyes were red and she had a calm smile. She only said that Andrés was tired, but that he had recognised her as soon as the door opened and had asked her whether she had brought her book. She had shown him the Romanian edition. He had shown her Rayuela, with the 1987 letter still kept between its pages.

In the hallway of the flat, by the green sign, Pilar was waiting; she had arrived from Seville the day before. The two women looked at each other for a moment. As a child, Pilar had hated the foreign woman who stole her father in the evenings; for years Ecaterina had envied that serious little girl who had the right to stay. Neither of them said anything. Then Pilar stepped forward and hugged her, and Ecaterina, who was not one for hugs, let herself be hugged for a long time.

The evening before the launch, the doctor called Marta. He had seen the weather forecast: thirty-four degrees were expected the next day. He reminded her of the conditions: if it was hot, Andrés couldn’t go. Marta called the fair’s director at ten at night. By half past ten, the launch had been moved from six in the evening to ten in the morning, the coolest time of day. The director told her that, for once, she didn’t mind bending the rules.

30 May dawned clear. At eight o’clock, the fair’s main marquee was already up, with three hundred plastic chairs and a long table covered with a green tablecloth, the same green as the bookshop sign. In the front row a space had been reserved with no chair, by the brightest window of the marquee, just as the director had promised in her January email. Above that space, someone had placed a small sign: “Reserved for the first reader”.

Costel and Andrei arrived at half past eight with the four boxes. They set them out at the publisher’s stand, among Spanish novels and cookery books. By nine a queue of a hundred people had already formed in front of the stand, although the launch didn’t start until ten. There were ladies with fans, students, elderly couples holding hands and a group of Romanians who lived in Madrid and had come with little flags.

While they were waiting, Costel received a video from Hungary. It was Zoltán, in the cab of his lorry, parked somewhere near Budapest, with the blue book in one hand and a handkerchief in the other. He had recorded a message in Spanish learnt by heart, word by word, with a terrible accent: “Many congratulations to Señor Andrés. I cry too.” Costel showed it to Marta. Marta said she would play it for her grandfather that very afternoon, and she was sure he would laugh.

Ecaterina, meanwhile, had sat down at one end of the long table, her hands on the book. Because of her cataracts, she saw the marquee as if through misted glass: patches of colour, shadows, lights. She told Ana it was better that way, because if she saw three hundred people looking at her clearly, she wouldn’t be able to read. Ana squeezed her hand and promised to whisper in her ear when Andrés arrived.

Andrés arrived at half past nine, in his wheelchair, pushed by Marta. He was wearing a linen jacket Pilar had bought him for the occasion and, on his knees, the two books: Rayuela and the Romanian edition. When he came into the marquee, a strange silence fell. Then someone started to clap. And then everyone. Three hundred people stood up. Andrés looked around, confused, and quietly asked Marta whether some minister had come.

Marta explained that the applause was for him. It took Andrés a while to understand. Then he did something nobody expected: he raised his right hand, as he used to in the bookshop when a regular customer came in, and greeted the audience with a small, elegant, old-fashioned bookseller’s gesture. The ovation lasted almost two minutes. Rosa Elena, sitting on Costel’s knees in the front row, clapped harder than anyone, although she didn’t really know why.

The launch was simple. Two passages were read: Marta read the first chapter in Spanish, the one about the bookshop on a rainy day, and Ecaterina read the last one in Romanian, the one about the morning the bookseller found a book left behind on the counter. Although most of the audience didn’t understand Romanian, nobody moved. All you could hear was Ecaterina’s voice, slow and firm, and now and then the distant noise of children playing in the park.

When Ecaterina had finished reading, she closed the book and turned to Andrés. She asked him, in Spanish, if he wanted to say something. Marta held the microphone up to him. Andrés looked at it for a long time, as if it were an unfamiliar object. The whole marquee held its breath. Everyone knew there were days when he couldn’t say a single sentence.

“In my bookshop,” he said at last, his voice weak but clear, “books were sold. But the best one was never sold. The best one was given away. And it was taken by a foreign woman who didn’t know what she was looking for.” He paused for a long time. “Forty years later, she has given it back to me. Translated. So it wasn’t such a bad deal after all.”

The marquee burst into laughter and applause at the same time. Costel was crying without the slightest attempt to hide it. Mihai passed a handkerchief to Ana, then another to Carmen, then another to Juan, and finally he ran out of handkerchiefs and had to use his shirt sleeve. Andrei took photos non-stop, although he later admitted half of them had come out blurred because his hands were shaking.

After the launch, Marta and Ecaterina signed books at the stand. The hundred Romanian copies sold out in twenty minutes, which hadn’t been expected, because it had been assumed most buyers would be Romanian and instead half of them were Spaniards who didn’t know a word of Romanian. One lady explained she was buying it to have it, even if she couldn’t read it. “It’s like having a love letter in a language you don’t understand,” she said. “You know what it says anyway.”

Costel, who had set aside a signed copy for his boss, one for his daughter and one for the mechanic from Maramureș who lived in Austria, was left with none for himself. When he realised, he went pale. Ecaterina, without a word, took out of her bag a copy she had hidden for him since Bucharest. On the first page she had written: “For Costel, who brought the books, the tears and the soup.”

At half past eleven the doctor gave the order: Andrés had to go home before the heat set in. They took him along the avenue in the Retiro, under the chestnut trees, Marta pushing the chair and Ecaterina walking beside him with her stick. Everyone else followed in silence, like a procession. Andrés asked them to stop for a moment by the lake. He looked at the water for a while. Then he told Ecaterina that it was there, in 1979, that he had first read her a poem aloud.

Ecaterina answered that she remembered. It was a poem by Machado. Andrés asked her to recite it. She hesitated, because she hadn’t read it in forty years. But she began, slowly, and the words came out one after another, as if they had been waiting for her. When she finished, Andrés had his eyes closed. For a moment Marta thought he had fallen asleep. But he said, without opening his eyes: “You skipped a line.” And he smiled.

That evening, at Carmen and Juan’s in Lavapiés, there was a dinner for everyone. Fourteen people crowded into a flat meant for four. They ate Mihai’s tortilla, with onion, sarmale that Ecaterina had brought frozen in her suitcase and Juan’s churros, which were cold by then but nobody complained. They drank a toast with Grandpa Gheorghe’s țuică, which Carmen tasted out of politeness and then asked for again out of conviction.

Around midnight, when almost everyone had gone, Ecaterina stayed for a moment on the balcony with Ana, looking at the rooftops of Lavapiés. Ana asked her how she felt. Ecaterina thought for a while. Then she said she felt like a book that has been finished: tired, complete and a little sad, because there were no pages left to write. Ana told her there were always pages left. Ecaterina smiled and replied that at her age pages are written more slowly, but they read better.
“apretara el calor” = the heat set in
